Timeline::searchsorted_left¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Series Timeline::searchsorted_left(const Timeline& values) const

Find The Start Of Each Insertion Range¶

searchsorted_left(values) performs binary searches in a sorted 1-D receiver. For every query timestamp, it returns the earliest position where that value could be inserted without disturbing ascending order.

If a query equals existing timestamps, the answer points before the first equal entry. If it falls between timestamps, the answer points at the later neighbor. Query NaT points to the beginning of the trailing NaT group.

The receiver and query play different shape roles: the receiver must be 1-D, but values may have any Timeline shape. The returned Int64 Series preserves the query shape.

Example 1: Search A Matrix Of Queries¶

const auto sorted = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-06-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-06-01T00:00:00Z", "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z", "", "",
});
const auto queries = pluss::timeline::make({
    {"2023-12-01T00:00:00Z", "2024-06-01T00:00:00Z"},
    {"2024-08-01T00:00:00Z", ""},
});
std::cout << pluss::series::print(sorted.searchsorted_left(queries)) << '\n';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 0 1 ⎤
⎣ 3 4 ⎦

The equal June query returns 1, before both matches. The absent query returns 4, before both trailing NaT entries.

Example 2: Use Both Sides As A Match Range¶

const auto key = pluss::timeline::make("2024-06-01T00:00:00Z");
const auto begin = sorted.searchsorted_left(key).item<std::int64_t>();
const auto end = sorted.searchsorted_right(key).item<std::int64_t>();
std::cout << "begin=" << begin << ", end=" << end
          << ", count=" << (end - begin) << '\n';

Output¶

begin=1, end=3, count=2

The half-open interval [begin, end) identifies every exact match without a linear scan.

Preconditions And Failure Modes¶

  • The receiver must be 1-D and already ascending with NaT last. Call sort() first when necessary.

  • The method does not sort or validate arbitrary receiver order.

  • The query may be scalar or N-D; only the receiver has the 1-D restriction.

  • Results are insertion positions, not proof that an exact match exists.

Summary¶

searchsorted_left() returns the first insertion boundary for each query, preserves query shape, and resolves ties and NaT to the left edge.
